title: uuid benchmark war
organization_author: Ardent Performance Computing blog (byline not captured)
engineering_principles: Time-ordered keys narrowed the insert gap to bigint in this test; bigint stayed smallest.
practical_examples: c7a.medium (1 core, 2 GB), gp3 16k IOPS, Ubuntu 22.04, PostgreSQL main branch of 2024-01-29 with v17 UUIDv7 patch, shared_buffers=1G, 20M initial rows, 1M inserted. uuid::text 410 s/2421 tps/4.31 GB; uuidv4 375 s/2670 tps/2.65 GB; uuidv7 290 s/3420 tps/2.47 GB; bigint 290 s/3480 tps/1.97 GB.
why_it_matters: Best published script for the three-way key comparison on PostgreSQL.
authority_rationale: Individual practitioner, but setup and copy-paste scripts are published; not peer reviewed.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. Pre-release patch, single small host, not PostgreSQL 18 GA. Employer and conflict of interest not established.

title: A deeper look at old UUIDv4 vs new UUIDv7 in PostgreSQL 18
engineering_principles: Random keys lower leaf density and destroy physical correlation.
practical_examples: PostgreSQL 18; hardware not stated. 50M into empty table: v4 1,239,840 ms, v7 106,343 ms. Next 50M: v4 2,776,881 ms, v7 100,354 ms. Index at 100M: 3,956 MB vs 3,008 MB. 1M rows pgstatindex: density 71 vs 89.98, fragmentation 49.99 vs 0.
why_it_matters: Largest PostgreSQL 18 data size found, and exposes index internals.
authority_rationale: Named specialist with SQL shown, but single-run, no hardware details; PostgreSQL services firm.
notes: Figures come from a WebFetch model summary only; curl of this page failed, so they are NOT confirmed against raw text. No bigint arm. Commercial interest: credativ sells PostgreSQL support. The post's prose ratios disagree with its own numbers, so use the raw timings.

title: UUIDv7 in Spring Boot and Postgres: The Right Way
organization_author: Coding Steve site (no byline; GitHub handle StevenPG)
engineering_principles: At small size on a laptop, v7 tracks bigint and v4 carries about 50 percent leaf fragmentation.
practical_examples: PostgreSQL 18 container on M-series MacBook, 1M rows, batches of 1,000. bigint 3,615 ms/21 MB; v7 3,820 ms/30 MB; v4 4,837 ms/38 MB.
why_it_matters: Only source found with all three key types on PostgreSQL 18 and a linked harness.
authority_rationale: Personal blog, laptop, 1M rows that likely fit in memory.
notes: Figures come from a WebFetch model summary only; curl of this page failed, so they are NOT confirmed against raw text. Repository github.com/StevenPG/DemosAndArticleContent (blog/uuidv7-spring-boot) was not opened. No conflict stated.

title: Storing UUID Values in MySQL
engineering_principles: Rearranging UUID bits to be time-ordered gave BIGINT-like insert and size behaviour.
practical_examples: 25M rows in batches of 25K; MySQL version and hardware not stated. .ibd size: ordered UUID 13 GB, BIGINT PK plus UUID index 15 GB, random UUID PK 20 GB. Insert times are charts only.
why_it_matters: Closest available InnoDB evidence for ordered versus random keys, predating UUIDv7.
authority_rationale: Recognised MySQL consultancy, SQL procedures shown; old and missing versions.
notes: Figures come from a WebFetch model summary only; curl of this page failed, so they are NOT confirmed against raw text. Percona sells MySQL services and distribution. Ordered UUID is a proxy for UUIDv7, not UUIDv7.

title: Illustrating Primary Key models in InnoDB and their impact on disk usage
engineering_principles: Random inserts leave leaf pages near half full.
practical_examples: About 60,880 records per test table. Leaf pages: AUTO_INCREMENT 99 at 90 percent fill; ordered binary(16) 147 at 91 percent; UUID() char(36) estimated 399 at slightly above 50 percent.
why_it_matters: Direct page-level picture of the mechanism behind the size difference.
authority_rationale: Vendor consultant, tiny test, mixes key type with key width.
notes: Figures come from a WebFetch model summary only; curl of this page failed, so they are NOT confirmed against raw text. Customer context was Percona Server 5.5; test server version not stated. No throughput measured.

title: Are MySQL UUID inserts really that slow?
engineering_principles: Under a tiny buffer pool, UUIDv1 matched INT while UUIDv4 fell away as the table grew.
practical_examples: MySQL 8.0.30, AMD EPYC 7642 4 vCPU, sysbench 16 threads, innodb_buffer_pool_size 64 MB. v4: INT(11) led CHAR(36) by over 2,000 inserts/s at 500 s (about 4M rows), nearly 4,000 at doubled duration (about 64M rows); p99 about 6x better for INT.
why_it_matters: Only MySQL 8 sysbench run with published Lua scripts found.
authority_rationale: Individual, but scripts and configuration are disclosed.
notes: Figures come from a WebFetch model summary only; curl of this page failed, so they are NOT confirmed against raw text. Linode supplied hosting credits. Repository github.com/obviyus/posts not opened. No UUIDv7 arm. The URL is a pages.dev mirror-style host.

title: Does Postgres RLS actually ruin performance? Let's look at the data.
engineering_principles: With a simple policy the index matters far more than policy evaluation.
practical_examples: 1M rows, one tenant about 10 percent, 50 runs less 3 warmup. p95 difference under 2 percent without index (count 73.3 ms vs 74.9 ms); with index count 2.2 ms vs 2.7 ms.
why_it_matters: Only opened RLS measurement with a controlled bypass comparison.
authority_rationale: Single developer post; PostgreSQL version, hardware and scripts not given.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. Single-condition policy only; subquery and join policies untested by the author's own statement. Author chose RLS for his platform before testing.

title: Foreign Keys vs Performance (Part 1): The INSERT Story
engineering_principles: Measured overhead depends on insert pattern; the small test does not show contention amplifying it.
practical_examples: PostgreSQL 16, unspecified dev machine, 100K users, 250K accounts, 5K merchants, 4 FKs, 1,000 operations. Without vs with FK: batch 114.2/151.6 ms; concurrent (10 threads) 817.2/818.5 ms; mixed 2,697.4/2,870.9 ms; sequential 5,012.4/5,286.2 ms.
why_it_matters: Only reproducible with/without FK harness found.
authority_rationale: Individual author with repository; small scale and a development machine.
notes: Figures come from a WebFetch model summary only; curl of this page failed, so they are NOT confirmed against raw text. Concurrent difference is well inside the reported error. Not at scale. Article mentions both .NET 8 and .NET 10, and states a batch overhead in seconds that disagrees with its 37.4 ms measurement. Repository github.com/Thyago-Oliveira-Perez/fk-benchmark not opened.

title: Data warehouse modeling: Star schema vs. OBT
subcategory: One Big Table vs star schema
engineering_principles: Flat tables were faster in BI-style queries at a large storage cost; results varied by engine.
practical_examples: TPC-DS scale 100 subset. Redshift dc2.large x1 and dc2.8xlarge x3, Snowflake X-Large, BigQuery default. OBT gain excluding Redshift compile: Redshift 25-30 percent, Snowflake about 25 percent, BigQuery about 50 percent. Redshift disk from just over 30 GB to over 90 GB.
authority_rationale: Scripts public; hosted by a data-pipeline vendor and only one author.
notes: Figures come from a WebFetch model summary only; curl of this page failed, so they are NOT confirmed against raw text. Conflict: published by Fivetran, whose product is not directly the tested warehouses. Repository github.com/mikekaminsky/compare-warehouse-distributions not opened. Engine versions are from 2022 and unstated.

title: A Performance Analysis for Efficient Schema Design in Cloud-Based Distributed Data Warehouses
organization_author: Fred E. R. Rabelo Ferreira and Robson do Nascimento Fidalgo, UFPE (ICEIS 2024)
subcategory: One Big Table vs star schema
engineering_principles: Denormalization is not a guaranteed gain; the winner depends on the engine.
practical_examples: SSB SF10 (60M rows) and SF50 (300M rows), 3 nodes with 16 GB RAM each on AWS. Star faster than flat by 74 percent on Redshift and 63 percent on MariaDB Columnstore; flat 42 percent faster on Singlestore. SF50 volume: Redshift 12.7 GB fact vs 62.7 GB flat.
why_it_matters: Strongest independent, peer-reviewed evidence on this question and contradicts vendor-hosted results.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed conference, university authors, states a public script; engine versions not found.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. Funding and conflict statement not located. Small clusters. The script location was not followed.

title: Varianten zur Speicherung multidimensionaler Daten: Star- und Snowflake-Schema, Column Stores und Data Vault
organization_author: Robert Schiller, University of Rostock (master's thesis)
engineering_principles: Star schema held the runtime and CPU advantage over Data Vault in this test.
practical_examples: SQL Server, Intel i5-3210M, 4 GB RAM, Windows 10 Pro laptop; SSB scale factor 1 (about 4.5 GB, LineOrder 6,001,215 rows). Per-query times appear in charts; the thesis notes only minimally worse Data Vault runtimes on the very small dataset and expects a worse result at larger size.
why_it_matters: Only direct Data Vault versus star measurement found.
authority_rationale: Supervised thesis, not peer reviewed; laptop and tiny data.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. SQL Server 2014 is named in the thesis's method section. Chart values were not transcribed. No conflict apparent.

title: The Performance of Anchor Model in Data Warehousing
organization_author: Rorimpandey et al., Universitas Negeri Manado (EIC 2018; published 2020)
engineering_principles: Reports no significant difference among Anchor, Data Vault and ONF, and a significant difference from star schema.
practical_examples: SQL Server, 13 information needs, Sidak test in GraphPad Prism 6. Timing values exist only in figures; version, hardware and data size not found in extracted text.
why_it_matters: Only published statistical comparison touching Data Vault; weak but must be recorded.
authority_rationale: Conference proceedings, setup not reproducible, and its conclusion that more joins run faster is implausible without controls.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. Treat as low-confidence. The conclusion favours more joins, which needs replication.

title: TiDB: A Raft-based HTAP Database
engineering_principles: Separate row and column replicas limit interference, at the cost of some replication lag.
practical_examples: Six servers, 188 GB, two E5-2630 v4 each. AP clients degraded TP at most 10 percent; TP degraded AP at most 5 percent. At 100 warehouses, under 1000 ms lag: 98.64-99.58 percent with 2 AP clients, 84.82-87.17 percent with 32. MemSQL 7.0 TP throughput fell by more than 5x with more AP clients.
why_it_matters: Rigorous design, but a vendor reporting on its own system.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed in PVLDB; full vendor conflict.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. NOT independent: all authors from PingCAP, and the competitor comparison is authored by the vendor.

title: HyBench: A New Benchmark for HTAP Databases
organization_author: Chao Zhang, Guoliang Li, Tao Lv (Tsinghua University, China Software Testing Center)
engineering_principles: Isolated architectures hold throughput and freshness better under concurrency; no architecture wins everywhere.
practical_examples: Four-node cluster, 40-core E5-2630, 128 GB, 1 TB SSD; SF1/10/100 (518 MB, 5.3 GB, 56 GB); PostgreSQL 14 streaming replication plus four anonymized commercial systems. SF1: PostgreSQL-SR H-Score 320, F-Score 24 ms; A4 QPS 676.29, XPS 45.49, F-Score 78 ms, H-Score 200. A4 ATS fell 7.99 to 1.08 at T-max with an F-Score of 19.6 s at (100,20).
why_it_matters: Best independent-leaning open benchmark for isolation and freshness, with public code.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed in PVLDB with public code; commercial systems anonymized.
notes: Figures confirmed against raw downloaded text. Conflict: supported partly by Huawei and CCF-Huawei fund; thanks GaussDB, OceanBase, Dameng, Alibaba Cloud and Tencent Cloud teams. Commercial systems unnamed due to DeWitt clauses, so results cannot be mapped to products. Repository github.com/Rucchao/HyBench-2023 not opened.

title: How Good is My HTAP System? (HATtrick; slides and code)
organization_author: Milkai et al., University of Wisconsin (SIGMOD 2022, DOI 10.1145/3514221.3526148)
engineering_principles: Isolation should be reported as a frontier of concurrent OLTP and OLAP throughput.
practical_examples: Combines an adapted TPC-C with SSB; code at github.com/UWHustle/HATtrick supports Postgres, TiDB and MySQL (Apache-2.0). No measured numbers recorded here.
why_it_matters: Canonical academic method for measuring isolation.
authority_rationale: SIGMOD academic method with open code; result numbers not verified here.
notes: Slides and repository were opened. The full paper at par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10390274 refused connections, so no results are recorded and none should be inferred. Funding or vendor ties not checked.
